kurz: How the assets and the equity and liabilities of a balance sheet show where a company's money is tied up and who is entitled to it.

bloecke.md:
A balance sheet shows the position on a single reporting date. It states what assets a company has and which part of them is due to the owners and which to the creditors. What happened between two reporting dates is shown in other parts of the annual financial statements.

The left-hand side, the assets (Aktiva), shows where the money is tied up. The right-hand side, equity and liabilities (Passiva), shows where it came from. Both sides describe the same amount from two directions and are therefore necessarily the same size. This total is called the [[Balance sheet total|balance sheet total]]. It indicates the size of a company and says nothing about its performance. A company can, for example, double its balance sheet total by taking out a loan and leaving the money in its account.

Section 266 HGB (Commercial Code) prescribes the horizontal account format and the order of items for corporations (Kapitalgesellschaften). Because they all use the same structure, the balance sheets of two different companies can be placed side by side and compared directly without first having to be rearranged.

bloecke.unter: Every euro on the equity and liabilities side is tied up in an item on the assets side. The figures come from the model balance sheet in this lesson, in € million.

bloecke.md:
## Fixed and current assets

The assets are ordered by increasing liquidity. At the top is what stays in the company longest.

**Fixed assets** are tied up permanently. They include intangible assets (purchased licences, patents, goodwill from acquisitions), tangible fixed assets (land, buildings, machinery) and long-term financial assets (equity investments, securities held for the long term). A company that sells any of these changes its business.

**Current assets** are turned over at least once a year. They include inventories, trade receivables, short-term securities, and cash and bank balances. Current bills are paid from these funds.

Below them come two items that are not assets in the everyday sense. Prepaid expenses (aktiver Rechnungsabgrenzungsposten) include, for example, rent paid in the old year for the new year. Deferred tax assets are an expected future tax benefit and not an object that could be sold. When assessing the asset base, you mentally deduct both items.

## Equity, provisions and liabilities

Equity is at the top because it stays in the company longest and, if things go wrong, is served last. It consists of subscribed capital (the nominal share capital), capital reserves (what shareholders have paid in above the nominal value), revenue reserves (profits retained from earlier years) and distributable profit (Bilanzgewinn). Equity is not a stock of cash lying somewhere. It is a calculated figure, namely assets minus debts.

**Provisions** are obligations that are uncertain as to their existence, amount or timing, such as pension commitments, warranties, pending lawsuits and decommissioning obligations. Their amount is based on estimates. Every estimate leaves leeway, and no other part of the balance sheet depends so heavily on judgement.

**Liabilities** are fixed in existence and amount. They include bonds, bank loans, unpaid supplier invoices and advance payments received. What matters with them is less the total than when they fall due. Under the HGB, the amount due within one year must be noted for each item (Section 268(5) HGB). An IFRS balance sheet usually separates current and non-current liabilities. More detailed information, such as the amount with a remaining maturity of more than five years, is given in the notes.

Under the HGB, pension obligations are discounted at the average market interest rate of the past ten financial years that corresponds to their remaining maturity. Alternatively, the rate for an assumed remaining maturity of 15 years may be used across the board (Section 253(2) HGB). Under IAS 19, by contrast, the reporting-date yield on high-quality corporate bonds applies. What is reported there is the net liability, that is, the present value of the obligation less the fair value of plan assets. Remeasurements are recognised in other comprehensive income and never in the income statement.

The same group can therefore report very different pension provisions under the HGB and under IFRS without any change in the pension commitments. The ten-year average smooths interest rate developments and therefore reacts to rate movements only with a lag of several years.

bloecke.md:
## Capital structure ratios

The first ratio is the [[Equity ratio|equity ratio]]. It indicates what proportion of the assets does not have to be repaid, and therefore how much loss a company can absorb before its creditors are affected. About 30% is considered sound. This figure is a convention from lending practice and is neither required by law nor a limit. Banks routinely operate with far less equity, because for them debt is part of the business itself and does not merely serve as financing.

The debt-to-equity ratio expresses the same thing differently, namely as debt divided by equity. A ratio of 2:1 corresponds to an equity ratio of about 33%.

bloecke.formel: Equity ratio = equity / balance sheet total × 100
bloecke.erklaerung: Indicates the proportion of the assets that belongs to the owners. The ratio is only comparable within a sector and within one accounting system.
variablen: item A on the equity and liabilities side, not the cash balance
total assets, equal to total equity and liabilities

bloecke.formel: Net financial debt = financial liabilities − cash and cash equivalents − short-term securities
bloecke.erklaerung: Shows how much interest-bearing debt would be left if the company used all its liquid funds to repay debt today. Pure trade payables are not included because they bear no interest.
bloecke.beispiel: (250 long-term + 60 short-term) − 70 cash − 10 securities = €230 million. Adding the pension provisions gives €380 million.

bloecke.md: Neither the HGB nor IFRS defines net debt. Some companies include pension provisions, others do not. Some deduct all securities, others only funds available daily. Since 2019, net debt at IFRS reporters has also included lease liabilities. Two groups in an identical position can therefore report very different net debt. Before any comparison, you should check the definition in the relevant annual report.

## Maturity matching and the golden balance sheet rule

The second thing to check is whether the maturities match. Assets tied up for the long term should be financed for the long term. Otherwise, for example, a factory building that lasts thirty years is financed with a loan that falls due in six months. Fixed asset coverage ratio II measures this relationship. It sets equity plus long-term debt against fixed assets. In the model balance sheet, that is 840 divided by 620, or 135.5%.

[[Working capital]], that is, current assets minus current liabilities, is the counterpart to this. It is the buffer with which day-to-day business is financed. In the model balance sheet, the short-term items are the bank liabilities of 60, trade payables of 140, other liabilities of 40 and tax provisions of 20, together 260. Working capital is therefore 470 − 260 = €210 million. The same 260 is the denominator of the three liquidity ratios (Liquiditätsgrade). The cash ratio sets only liquid funds against it, the quick ratio adds receivables and short-term securities, and the current ratio uses all current assets. Negative working capital is not automatically bad. In food retail and subscription models it is the rule, because customers pay before suppliers are paid. With long production cycles and no advance payments, on the other hand, negative working capital is a warning sign.

bloecke.md:
## Goodwill

If a group buys another company for more than its remeasured net assets are worth, the difference is capitalised as [[Goodwill (Geschäfts- oder Firmenwert)|goodwill]]. It stands for brand, customer base and hoped-for synergies, that is, for expectations the buyer has paid for. A company may never recognise goodwill it has built up itself on its balance sheet. Section 248(2) HGB also expressly prohibits capitalising internally generated brands, mastheads, publishing rights and customer lists, and IAS 38 prohibits the same items. This creates an asymmetry. A company that grows through acquisitions has a high balance sheet total and an equity ratio that looks respectable. A company that has built up the same brand itself reports a smaller balance sheet.

The HGB and IFRS differ in subsequent measurement. Under the HGB, acquired goodwill is amortised on a scheduled basis, over ten years if its useful life cannot be estimated reliably (Section 253(3) HGB). Under IFRS, it is not amortised on a scheduled basis. Instead, an impairment test under IAS 36 is required at least once a year, and an impairment loss, once recognised, may never be reversed.

Goodwill generates no cash flows of its own and cannot be sold separately. The usual stress test therefore deducts it from equity, together with capitalised development costs, which are likewise only worth something as long as the project works.

bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation. After deducting goodwill and capitalised development costs, the equity ratio falls from 35.0% to 23.5%.

bloecke.md:
## Hidden reserves and hidden burdens

Under the HGB, acquisition or production cost forms the upper limit of valuation. A plot of land bought fifty years ago therefore still appears on the balance sheet today at its historical cost, even if it is now worth many times as much. A machine that has been fully depreciated on schedule but will run for another twelve years appears on the balance sheet only at a token value. The difference between book value and real value is called [[Hidden reserves|hidden reserves]]. It is real wealth that does not show up in any ratio. The HGB deliberately accepts this to protect creditors and would rather make a company look poorer than richer.

Hidden burdens (stille Lasten) are the reverse case. Examples are inventories that can no longer be sold, equity investments whose business has collapsed, and provisions that are too low. They only become visible when a write-down is made, which is usually too late.

IFRS takes the opposite approach. In several places it permits fair values instead of historical cost and thus shows more of the current value, but also values that fluctuate more. The HGB and IFRS financial statements of the same group differ systematically in goodwill, development costs, leasing and pensions. Equity ratios from the two sets of rules cannot be meaningfully compared without a reconciliation.

For financial years beginning on or after 1 January 2019, a lessee under IFRS 16 must recognise practically every lease on its balance sheet. It records a right-of-use asset on the assets side and a lease liability on the equity and liabilities side. Exceptions apply only to terms of up to twelve months and to low-value assets.

As a result, the balance sheet total and net debt rise and the equity ratio falls, without anything having changed in the business. For retail chains, airlines and restaurant companies, the effect was considerable. Time series spanning 2019 are not comparable on this point without adjustment.

That assets and equity and liabilities are equal in size follows from the definition of the balance sheet and is not a finding about the company. What is informative are the proportions within each side, the comparison with the same company's previous years and the question of what happened to look favourable on the reporting date, whether by chance or by design.

bloecke.md:
The scope of the financial statements, the audit requirement and disclosure depend on the size class under Section 267 HGB. Three criteria are decisive, namely balance sheet total, revenue and the average number of employees over the year. Two of them must be exceeded, or not reached, on two consecutive balance sheet dates.

- Micro company (Section 267a HGB): €450,000 balance sheet total, €900,000 revenue, 10 employees
- Small: €7.5 million balance sheet total, €15 million revenue, 50 employees
- Medium-sized: €25 million balance sheet total, €50 million revenue, 250 employees

A company that exceeds at least two of the thresholds for medium-sized companies is a large corporation. Small companies are not subject to a statutory audit and may publish abridged accounts; micro companies may largely dispense with the notes. The amounts were raised by about 25% for inflation by Delegated Directive (EU) 2023/2775. They apply to financial years beginning on or after 1 January 2024.

In practice, the published accounts of a small GmbH (private limited company) therefore often consist only of an abridged balance sheet without an income statement. What is not there cannot be reconstructed either.

mitnehmen: The assets side shows where the money is tied up, the equity and liabilities side who is entitled to it. The balance sheet total indicates size and says nothing about performance.
The equity ratio is the most important structural ratio. How robust it is only becomes clear from the calculation after deducting goodwill and capitalised development costs.
Provisions are based on estimates. Pension provisions depend on the discount rate and differ systematically between the HGB and IFRS.
Rules of thumb such as a 30% equity ratio or 100% fixed asset coverage II are conventions of practice, not limits.
The balance sheet only shows what has been paid for. Internally built brands are missing, as are hidden reserves, and the balance sheet on the reporting date can be window-dressed.

begriffe.text: The sum of all assets, identical to the sum of all equity and liabilities. It measures the size of the capital employed, not success.

Equity divided by the balance sheet total. The ratio shows what proportion of the assets does not have to be repaid. By common convention, about 30% is considered sound, but the appropriate level depends heavily on the sector.
Interest-bearing financial liabilities less cash and cash equivalents and short-term securities. The figure is not defined by law, so companies treat pensions and leases differently.
Current assets minus current liabilities. It serves as a buffer for day-to-day business. A negative value can be normal or dangerous, depending on the business model.

The capitalised excess that a buyer has paid over the remeasured net assets of the acquired company. Under the HGB it must be amortised on a scheduled basis; under IFRS it must be tested for impairment every year.
The difference between the book value of an item and its real value. It arises from the historical cost principle and from scheduled depreciation and is not visible in any ratio.
